overview: Ethiopia’s history includes a long-lived empire and later governments, alongside communities with distinct languages, religions and institutions. Abyssinia was a European name used for the empire. Manuscripts, buildings, farming landscapes and living craft traditions reveal histories that cannot be reduced to the careers of emperors.

periods.title: Imperial patronage and monastic learning
periods.summary: The Ethiopian Empire supported Christian monasteries as centres of learning and manuscript production. Surviving Gospel books reveal relationships between religious scholarship, visual art and elite patrons.

periods.title: Gondar and changing royal authority
periods.summary: Fasilidas established a permanent capital at Gondar in 1636. Palaces, libraries, churches and other buildings grew around the court. Its later political decline did not end Gondar’s commercial or religious life.

periods.title: Rebuilding and expanding imperial power
periods.summary: Tewodros II began a renewed project of imperial consolidation in 1855. Later rulers extended state power, with religious policy closely entwined with political authority.

periods.title: Iyasu and contested succession
periods.summary: Iyasu sought support across religious constituencies, including Muslim politicians. His rivals used accusations of conversion against him; whether he converted remains disputed.

periods.title: Zewditu and Tafari
periods.summary: Zewditu became empress in 1916, with Tafari Makonnen as regent and heir. Their partnership contained competing approaches to imperial government.

periods.title: Haile Selassie’s early reign
periods.summary: Haile Selassie became emperor in 1930 and pursued reforms before Italy’s invasion in 1935.

periods.title: Italian occupation and resistance
periods.summary: Italian occupation displaced the emperor, but never brought all the countryside under Italian control.

periods.title: Restored imperial government
periods.summary: Haile Selassie resumed rule. Centralisation and reforms coexisted with growing opposition and the crisis of famine.

periods.title: Military rule under the Derg
periods.summary: The Derg replaced the emperor in 1974. Warfare and armed opposition culminated in the regime’s collapse in 1991.

periods.title: Transition to a new constitutional order
periods.summary: A transitional government followed the Derg’s defeat. A constituent assembly adopted a new federal constitution in December 1994.

periods.title: A federal republic
periods.summary: A new government took office in August 1995 under the federal constitution. This institutional change followed the earlier end of imperial rule.

items.text: A Gospel manuscript now at the Metropolitan Museum dates from the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century. Its parchment pages combine Ge’ez text with painted Gospel scenes. The museum identifies two artists, whose shared visual language transformed models connected to the eastern Mediterranean.

The book was made at a northern Ethiopian monastic centre. A possible connection to Dabra Hayg Estifanos is a scholarly attribution, not a recorded excavation find. Notes associate its recipient church with the Archangel Michael, while the paintings were intended for viewing during worship and processions.

The late seventeenth-century Arganonä Maryam prayer book organises prayers using decorated headings for days of the week. Geometric borders help readers navigate the text. Its parchment, pigments, script and binding required several kinds of practical skill as well as religious learning.

Pencil additions, erased and rewritten red text, and smudges reveal the prayer book’s later use. Its colophon names Baselyos, but scholars debate whether the scribe also painted the hornbill image associated with this group of manuscripts. Evidence of authorship is therefore more complex than one modern artist label.

Fasil Ghebbi’s royal compound contains more than castles. Its surviving structures include a library, a chancellery and a banqueting hall, alongside palaces and nearby churches. The ensemble shows how a settled court brought administration, ceremony and skilled construction into a permanent urban centre.

At the Bath of Fasilidas, a canal carried water from the nearby river into a rectangular pool around a pavilion. The building stands on pier arches and was reached by a stone bridge. Water supply and structural engineering were integral to the royal landscape.

Konso communities shaped steep land with dry-stone terraces that retain soil, collect rainfall and discharge excess water. Their maintenance depends on organised communal labour. These southern Ethiopian landscapes represent local environmental knowledge rather than a technology that can be credited to the imperial dynasty.

Within Konso settlements, communal spaces called moras organise social and ceremonial life. Reservoirs are built and maintained collectively, while generation-marking stones record transfers of responsibility. Farming infrastructure and local institutions belong to the same cultural landscape.

Designer Hana Getachew describes Habesha dresses made from fine cotton with coloured geometric decoration called tibeb. On a simple two-harness loom, artisans must pick decorative patterns by hand or add embroidery. The cloth’s apparent lightness conceals patient, technically demanding work.

At the contemporary Sabahar workshop, local women spin cotton by hand, yarn is dyed, and weavers thread the loom before weaving panels. Washing and careful stitching finish the cloth. Getachew’s account links design, distributed labour and changing markets without implying that all Ethiopian households follow this practice.

The Oromo Gada system provides a distinct tradition of community governance. Assemblies and elected leadership address administration, disputes and social responsibilities, while knowledge is passed between generations. It operates at a local level and should not be confused with the institutions of Ethiopia’s imperial or federal governments.

Haile Selassie’s 1931 constitution drew on foreign constitutional models but strengthened imperial authority. Written government rules did not necessarily mean independent parliamentary power. This distinction helps explain why institutional reform and political participation did not always advance together.

Menelik II’s army defeated the Italian invasion at Adwa in 1896. His reign also brought conquest and annexation in the south. Resistance to European colonial rule and expansion over neighbouring communities were different processes within the same imperial history.

The constitution adopted in December 1994 speaks in the name of Ethiopia’s nations, nationalities and peoples, emphasising equality and shared political life. Its wording records the new constitutional project; it is not proof that subsequent governments fulfilled every stated aim.

ending.text: The emperor was removed in September 1974 and the Derg assumed power. That ended imperial government, not Ethiopia or its peoples. The Derg itself fell in 1991, followed by a transitional administration and a federal republic. These regime changes must be distinguished from the country’s continuing history.
